page: Google Cloud Platform n4d-highmem-16 is a dedicated virtual machine instance based on the x86_64 architecture, configured with 16 dedicated vCPUs and 128 GB of system memory. This configuration provides a high memory allocation of 8 GB per core, targeting scenarios that require substantial memory capacity relative to compute capacity. The instance includes no integrated GPUs and supplies zero local storage, requiring attached persistent storage volumes for operating system disks and data storage.

The resource distribution emphasizes cost efficiency for memory-bound tasks by delivering a 1:8 vCPU-to-RAM proportion without forcing provisioning of unneeded additional processor cores. As an instance without bundled ephemeral NVMe storage or bundled complimentary public IPv4 addresses, network and storage architectures depend entirely on Google Cloud virtual networking and persistent disk infrastructure. Dedicated core assignment ensures predictable performance free from multi-tenant CPU throttling.

The n4d-highmem-16 instance is suited for memory-intensive enterprise applications, relational database engines, Redis and Memcached caching tiers, and medium-scale extract, transform, and load pipelines.
description: Google Cloud Platform n4d-highmem-16 is a dedicated virtual machine offering 16 x86_64 vCPUs paired with 128 GB of system memory, yielding an 8 GB per vCPU ratio. Designed for high memory demands within general-purpose compute deployments, the machine features dedicated virtual cores to maintain steady processing performance without resource contention. The instance does not include bundled local storage or integrated GPU accelerators, meaning workloads rely entirely on attached network-based block storage and standard host compute resources. By providing 128 GB of RAM across a 16-thread envelope, the server delivers resource efficiency for applications that exhaust memory before utilizing excessive core counts. The n4d-highmem-16 configuration is well tailored for enterprise application servers, in-memory caches, relational database systems, and data transformation jobs that require substantial working memory buffers.
